subject: Computer Networking
title: Undersea Cables
description: A quick, practical guide to Undersea Cables.

hook.text: There are over 500 cables on the ocean floor right now, carrying 99% of intercontinental data.

buildup.text: Each cable is a bundle of fiber optic strands, armored in steel and plastic, laid by specialized ships.

discovery.text: Repeaters every 50 miles boost the light signal so it can cross entire oceans without fading.

twist.text: Anchors, earthquakes, and even sharks have damaged cables. Redundancy is the only real protection.

climax.text: When a cable to Tonga was cut in 2022, the entire country lost internet for weeks.

punchline.text: The cloud isn't in the sky. It's under the sea.

quiz.question: What carries most intercontinental internet traffic?

details.summary: Undersea fiber optic cables carry over 95 percent of intercontinental internet traffic along the ocean floor. These cables are thin but carry enormous bandwidth using wavelength-division multiplexing. They are laid by specialized ships and are vulnerable to anchors, earthquakes, and sabotage.
details.whyItMatters: The global internet depends on undersea cables. Understanding this reveals why certain regions lose connectivity during natural disasters or geopolitical conflicts.
takeaways: Over 95% of international internet traffic uses undersea cables
Cables are laid on the ocean floor by specialized ships
They are vulnerable to anchors, earthquakes, and sabotage

faq.question: How many undersea cables exist?
faq.answer: Over 500 submarine cables are in operation, totaling more than 1.4 million kilometers. New cables are constantly being laid as bandwidth demand grows. Google, Meta, and Microsoft are among the largest investors in new submarine cable projects.

faq.question: Are satellites a viable alternative to undersea cables?
faq.answer: Satellites cannot match undersea cable bandwidth and have much higher latency for geostationary orbits. Low-earth orbit constellations like Starlink improve latency but still cannot match cable capacity. Satellites complement cables for reaching remote areas but will not replace them.
